title: Salt Typhoon
summary: Salt Typhoon is a China linked espionage group that public reporting places inside the networks of major telecommunications carriers, including providers in the United States and other regions. Rather than ransomware or disruption, its apparent aim is collection. Reported activity focuses on routers, switches, lawful interception and call detail systems, because those positions expose communications content, metadata and subscriber records. Public reporting describes long dwell time, use of living off the land techniques and built in device features, credential theft from configuration stores, and quiet movement between carrier networks. Evidence lives in network device configuration and command logs, authentication events from unusual sources, changes to routing or interception settings, and downstream flow records. Attribution to a state sponsor comes from infrastructure and target pattern analysis in public reporting and is presented with varying degrees of confidence.

beginner.definition: Salt Typhoon is a team of spies that breaks into telephone and internet companies. Experts link this group to China in public reports. Instead of locking files, they stay hidden and copy information that passes through the network.
beginner.whyItMatters: Phone and internet providers carry everyone's calls, messages and account records. If an intruder sits inside that network, they may read who contacted whom, when, and sometimes what was said. A telephone network is huge and full of old equipment that few people watch closely. One quiet intruder in the wrong place can affect millions of ordinary people at once.
howItWorks: They study the phone company from outside and look for weak or exposed devices.
They steal an administrator account from a router or a management system.
They change the device setup so they keep access after a reboot.
They collect call records, messages and login data as it moves past them.
They move to other carriers that share links or trust with the first one.
They hide inside normal traffic, so the network keeps working as usual.
beginner.example: Imagine the switchboard of a large old hotel. Every call and every note passes through the same room. An intruder does not close the hotel or break the phones. He simply sits in the back room with a notepad, reading the register, and puts his own copy of the master key on a hook so he can return whenever he likes.
takeaways: Telecom networks carry metadata, which is often as sensitive as content.
Router and switch logs matter, because antivirus on laptops cannot see them.
Attribution in public reporting is based on patterns and stays uncertain.

objectives: Explain why telecommunications carriers are a high value espionage target.
Describe how network device configuration changes can provide durable attacker access.
List the log sources that would help detect an intrusion in a carrier network.
Compare a collection focused intrusion with a disruptive ransomware intrusion.
State the limits of public attribution for a state linked intrusion set.
